extracted.intended_audience: students/scholars/practitioners of humour theory, playwrights and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic theory and criteria for producing and recognising the comic in language, situation and character, as found in a classic philosophical essay on laughter. Aims to delineate mechanisms (inversion, transposition, exaggeration, automatism, etc.) and conditions under which things become laughable.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comic Transformation of Sentences (three laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: A phrase is likely to become comic if, though reversed, it still makes sense, or if it expresses equally well two quite independent sets of ideas, or if it has been obtained by transposing an idea into some key other than its own. These are the three fundamental laws of THE COMIC TRANSFORMATION OF SENTENCES.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three laws are: INVERSION (reversing sentence roles), RECIPROCAL INTERFERENCE (bracketing two independent meanings in the same expression), and TRANSPOSITION (placing an idea in another key). The page illustrates each with examples and notes varying importance (inversion least important, transposition most far-reaching).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce a comic effect by reversing elements of a sentence (e.g., putting subject in place of object and vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the least interesting of the three sentence-transformations but easy to apply; example provided (Labiche comedy exchange). Often used to refute an idea in humorous terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference / Pun vs Play upon Words
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce two independent meanings within the same sentence so they interfere with one another; this includes puns and true plays upon words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes the pun (two different sentences with same sound) from a true play upon words (one sentence expressing two idea-sets via multiple meanings); play upon words often signals a 'LAPSE OF ATTENTION' in language and is amusing for that negligence. Examples and gradations provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition (language into another key)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain comic effect by transposing the natural expression of an idea into another key or environment (language itself playing a comedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule given explicitly: 'A COMIC EFFECT IS ALWAYS OBTAINABLE BY TRANSPOSING THE NATURE EXPRESSION OF AN IDEA INTO ANOTHER KEY.' Transposition ranges from buffoonery to refined irony; many applications and stages are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition as comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition consists in arranging events so that a scene is reproduced in another key — e.g., between same characters in fresh circumstances or new characters in same circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called the favourite method of classic comedy; transposition in language is likened to repetition in situation. Used to highlight contrast between original and transposed versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody (solemn → familiar transposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transpose the solemn into the familiar to produce parody; expressing old-world/classical matters in modern or trivial terms yields comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Jean Paul Richter's dawn simile 'like a lobster being boiled.' Parody is presented as a form of transposition sometimes analysed as 'degradation'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degradation / Exaggeration (transposition downward)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposition from better to worse (degradation) or speaking of small things as though large (exaggeration) produces comic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration is especially comic when prolonged/systematic (mock-heroic). Degradation and exaggeration are presented as specific forms of transposition with historical examples (mock-heroic poems, braggadocio).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition upwards (moral upscaling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe low or disreputable matters in highly respectable language (transposition upwards of moral value) to create comic contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often brief wording suffices (a single word can reveal a whole system of transposition). Example: Gogol-like official saying 'Your peculations are too extensive for an official of your rank.' Noted as a characteristically English practice in literature (Dickens, Thackeray).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast between Real and Ideal: Irony vs Humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposition between what is and what ought to be yields IRONY (pretend to believe the ideal is actual) or HUMOUR (describe the actual as if it were the ideal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony is 'oratorical' and may become impassioned; humour is 'scientific', delighting in concrete terms and technical detail. Humour is described as a transposition from the moral to the scientific and as the counterpart of irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional/Technical Jargon Transposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposing everyday ideas into the technical vocabulary or business phraseology of a profession yields comic results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: business phrase 'Your kindness of the third ult.' applied to social invitations; transposition can reveal faults of character when professional language is applied to personal relations (Labiche, Famille Benoiton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic is linked to Social Unsociability
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic expresses a special lack of adaptability to society—unsociability—so any individual who goes his own way without adapting may become comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter functions as social 'ragging' or corrective humiliation. Comedy is neither wholly art nor wholly life; it implies a social intent to humiliate or correct the neighbour's absentmindedness or rigidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity / Ready-made / Automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Ready-made, mechanical, stereotyped elements of personality (rigidity, automatism, habits) are prime material for comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language and character that are 'ready-made' invite comic manipulation; the more stereotyped and automatic a trait, the more comic it is. Such elements allow imitation and the formation of stock types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absentmindedness and Systematic Absentmindedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Absentmindedness—unwitting actions, involuntary gestures, oblivious contradictions—is especially comical; systematic absentmindedness is the most comical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profoundly comic sayings are artless remarks where a vice reveals itself nakedly; examples include Don Quixote and characters who contradict their stated positions by their deeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gesture over Action
rubrics_metrics.description: To create comedy, direct attention to gestures (attitudes, movements, language as automatic) rather than to intentional actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action is conscious and binds the whole person; gesture is automatic/explosive and isolates a part, preventing emotional engagement. Comedy utilises gestures to rouse sensibility and avoid seriousness (Tartuffe example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation of feeling (parasitic feeling) to avoid emotional contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a character's feeling 'parasitic'—rigidly isolated within the soul—so it fails to spread and thus does not arouse sympathy, enabling comic reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotions that are dramatic are contagious; to prevent sympathy, the comic poet isolates feelings so they remain rigid and puppet-like. Harpagon's greed example shows a feeling that passes without touching other feelings (hence comic rather than tragic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary condition: must not arouse spectator's emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: For a vice or situation (even serious ones) to be laughable, it must not arouse the spectator's feelings; emotional engagement precludes laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the 'sole condition really necessary' though not sufficient. The comic poet uses methods (isolation, gesture, parody, transposition) to lull sensibility or to dampen sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as Types / Stock Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy depicts the ready-made element of personality as general types; every comic character is a type and comedy aims at the general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the mechanical element of personality is imitable and repeatable, comedy crystallises characters into categories that others can fall into; this generality distinguishes comedy from other arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of comic in words, situation and character
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic in language follows the comic in situation and merges with the comic in character; all three interact and reinforce laughability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language attains laughable results because it is modelled on human mind; defects like automatism and absentmindedness appear across words, actions and character, and are the elements laughter singles out.
